The question of whether humans can live to over 150 years is genuinely contested among researchers. Some studies strongly suggest a hard biological ceiling well below 150: a study published in Nature found that maximum human age plateaued around 115 after 1995, with the odds of anyone living past 125 in any given year at less than 1 in 10,000 [d6], and research published in Nature also suggests there is a limit to human lifespan and that breaking Calment's record of 122 is unlikely [d2]. The longest verified human lifespan remains Jeanne Calment's 122 years and 5 months [d9]. On the other hand, a University of Georgia researcher argues humans are "not even close" to reaching the maximum potential lifespan, with people possibly reaching 150 [d4], and Dr. Andrew Steele, a computational biologist, states there is "no biological reason humans can't reach the age of 200," believing someone alive today could reach 150 with the help of drugs currently in human trials [d10]. Several studies from Gero treat 150 as an upper ceiling set by the loss of physiological resilience, rather than a realistic target under current conditions [d5][d7][d8], while GERO.AI's analysis of 70,000 participants found none showed the biological resiliency to actually reach 150 [d1][d3]. In summary, current evidence places 150 years as a theoretical upper boundary that no human has yet approached, with sharp disagreement over whether future medicine could make it achievable.
